title: Egress NAT Gateway handshake investigation notes
content:
One-off scratchpad for the NAT gateway / TLS handshake flakiness reported from customer A (private deployment). High-level symptom: intermittent TLS handshake failures when connecting to external model hosts (port 443), but only from a subset of instances in the VPC. Failures reproduce from some AZs and not others. Notes, commands, outputs, and hypotheses below - chronological and raw.

Top-level hypothesis summary (current):
- Likely interaction between VPC peering + NAT Gateway + MTU/path MTU + occasional ICMP blackhole causing TLS handshake stalls (SYN/ACK + TLS ClientHello fragmentation) OR
- Source NAT port exhaustion / conntrack entries causing reset of flows on long-lived connections; but failures occur on new connections too so less likely.
- Possible DPI / corporate edge doing TLS inspection on egress paths (less likely for customer private deployments, but observed in similar cases).

Quick commands run (ssh into affected instance ip-10-0-43-22):
- ip route show: 
  default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100
  10.0.0.0/16 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.43.22
- sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward -> 0 (expected for regular instance)
- cat /etc/resolv.conf -> nameserver 169.254.169.253 / stub resolver to VPC provided
- dig +tcp model-host.example.com @169.254.169.253 -> returns 3 A records, TTL 300

Reproducing a failure (from this instance):
- curl -v --connect-timeout 10 https://models.example.com/health
  * Rebuilt URL to: https://models.example.com/health
  *   Trying 203.0.113.21:443...
  * TCP_NODELAY set
  * Connected to models.example.com (203.0.113.21) port 443 (#0)
  * TLS handshake: error:1408F10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_record:wrong version number
  * Closing connection 0
  curl: (35) error:1408F10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_record:wrong version number

- openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.21:443 -servername models.example.com -alpn h2
  CONNECTED(00000003)
  140123456789024:error:14077410:SSL routines:SSL23_GET_SERVER_HELLO:sslv3 alert handshake failure:../ssl/s23_clnt.c:770:
  ---
  no peer certificate available
  ---
  No client certificate CA names sent
  ---
  SSL handshake has read 7 bytes and written 313 bytes
  ---
  
  # Note: small read -> server closed quickly.

From another instance in same subnet/AZ (10.0.43.55) at same moment: curl succeeds, full handshake and HTTP 200. So not all traffic to that external IP is failing.

Network trace (tcpdump) while reproducing: tcpdump -nni eth0 host 203.0.113.21 and port 443 -w /tmp/handshake.pcap
- Observed: SYN -> SYN/ACK -> ACK -> TLS ClientHello (len ~512) -> no server handshake response, finally RST from server after ~8s. When capture taken from a healthy instance, we see full TLS ServerHello etc.

Exported pcap and compared:
- Failed flow: ClientHello appears in a single TLS record, but packet length is fragmented across IP fragments? Not typical for MTU 1500. Need to inspect IP flags (DF set?)
- Healthy flow: ClientHello arrives and server responds in < 150ms.

Hypothesis: Path MTU + DF interactions or intermediate appliance dropping fragmented IP packets. If ClientHello is larger (SNI + ALPN + cert compression + large cipher list), and if DF is set and path MTU smaller than 1500 somewhere (peering link or transit), then packets get dropped by a blackhole and server never sees ClientHello; but we observe server did see something (RST) -> server may be rejecting because it got truncated/garbled handshake.

Commands to inspect MTU / fragmentation: 
- ip link show eth0 -> mtu 9001 (we use jumbo in this VPC)
- ping -M do -s 1472 203.0.113.21 -> "packets need to be fragmented but DF set" (fails)
- traceroute -F -n -w 2 203.0.113.21 shows one hop outside 10.0.0.0/16 then timed out at transit.
- sudo sysctl net.ipv4.ip_no_pmtu_disc -> 0 (PMTU discovery enabled)

AWS-side checks: 
- aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters "Name=status-code,Values=active" shows peering to partner-vpc-12345 in another account but only used for private subnets; not sure it's used for this egress path.
- aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc shows default route to NAT gateway nat-0a1b2c3d in public subnet 10.0.1.0/24
- NAT gateway attach/enis show: nat-0a1b2c3d has ENI in public-subnet-1 (mtu=1500) while our instances have jumbo (9001) -> possible mismatch.

Interesting note: Instances have MTU 9001 but NAT gateway ENI is 1500. Normally AWS handles fragmentation, but with DF set and PMTU issues, large client hello might be fragmented before NAT and get dropped. Also VPC peering between customer account and partner networks may add additional MTU constraints.

Other commands run to test TLS size sensitivity: 
- curl -v --ciphers "ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256" --tlsv1.2 https://models.example.com/health -> reduces ClientHello size a bit, sometimes succeeds.
- curl -v --http1.1 https://models.example.com/health -> smaller than http2 ClientHello? intermittent success.
- curl -v --header "Host: models.example.com" --resolve models.example.com:443:203.0.113.21 https://models.example.com/health -> same behavior as before.

Conntrack / ephemeral ports checks: 
- sudo conntrack -L | grep 203.0.113.21 -> only 2 entries when testing (no explosion).
- ss -tn sport = :443 shows few ephemeral connections. No exhaustion.

Iptables and host firewall: 
- sudo iptables -S -> default ACCEPT rules, no rate limiting, no mangle table rules observed.

Other reproducibility notes:
- Failures mostly from instances launched earlier (2024-12- image) vs newly provisioned ones (2025-10-). Could be instance AMI network config default mtu changed.
- Instances with failure have /etc/sysctl.d/90-redwood-network.conf forcing mtu 9001 at boot via ip link set dev eth0 mtu 9001. Older instances have that; newer ones default to 1500.

Mitigation attempts executed: 
1) Force MTU to 1500 on affected instance: sudo ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1500; then curl -> success repeatedly.
   - Temporarily fixes the issue on that instance.
2) On the server side we can't change remote. Engaged customer contact to ask their infra team if they see TLS handshake anomalies for specific source IPs. They reported seeing ClientHello that looks truncated for those failing IPs.
3) Tried forcing TLS options to reduce ClientHello size (disable ALPN, limit ciphers) -> reduced failure rate but not zero.

Conclusion so far: Strong evidence that MTU mismatch between instance (9001) and egress NAT ENI (1500) / transit path is the proximate cause. Likely sequence: instance sends large TCP segments (with DF) expecting path to support jumbo frames; IP fragmentation or drop at NAT/transit causes truncated ClientHello server rejects. Because PMTU discovery depends on ICMP unreachable which might be blocked, the sender doesn't know to reduce MSS.

Action items (next):
- Short term: Update affected instances to default to 1500 MTU in AMI bootstrap to avoid regression (done for new AMI). Roll a fix script to change MTU on running fleet as a hotfix.
- Mid term: Add monitoring that tracks TLS ClientHello length distribution and handshake success rate per subnet/AZ to detect regressions.
- Long term: Validate and document expected MTU across private deployments and enforce parity between instance MTU and NAT gateway/transit. Add an infra check in our onboarding playbook (check ENI MTU vs instance mtu).

Notes for postmortem:
- Root cause: Instance MTU mismatch (9001) vs egress path MTU (1500) leading to fragmented/blocked TLS ClientHello.
- Why not immediately obvious: Many connections are smaller than threshold or success depends on server's MSS handling, so failures are intermittent and AZ/ENI-dependent.
- Detection: customer reported TLS handshake timeouts; internal debugging traced to MTU.

Interesting edge-case to document: some flows succeeded despite jumbo MTU because kernel performed TCP segmentation offload (TSO/GSO) in a way that produced smaller on-wire frames; differences in NIC drivers and virtualized hardware affected when fragmentation occurred. That explains instance-generation correlation.

Random command snippets I saved during debugging (keep for breadcrumbs):
- sudo ethtool -k eth0 | egrep -i "gso|gro|tso"
- sudo iptables -t mangle -vnL POSTROUTING
- sudo tcpdump -nni eth0 "tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) != 0 and host 203.0.113.21" -w /tmp/handshake.pcap
- sudo tc qdisc show dev eth0

Slack refs: #private-deploy (thread id: t-kwjn3) - shared pcap and curl logs.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Is there any AWS doc that guarantees NAT gateway ENI MTU is 1500? Need concrete citation.
- Do we need to proactively set instance MTU to 1500 in all private deployments? Risk: slightly higher overhead but avoids handshake failures.
- Could we detect this automatically (e.g., probe to a known external host with artificially large ClientHello to see if failures occur)? Possibly add a small synthetic check in health probes.

Appendix - quick checklist to reproduce locally:
1) Launch instance with mtu 9001 in private subnet routed through NAT gateway.
2) curl to large-TLS-server (models.example.com) with http2 enabled; observe handshake failure.
3) change mtu to 1500, test again -> handshake succeeds.

End of notes.

(If I come back to this later, check: aws documented MTU for NAT gateway, partner-vpc peering mtu interplay, any network middleboxes doing TLS inspection, and double-check kernel GSO/TSO behavior differences across instance types.)
